docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
The purpose of this repository is to implement a Customer 360 streaming data pipeline integrating operational databases (PostgreSQL, DB2,...) with event streaming, Change Data Capture (CDC), and modern lakehouse analytical sinks.

This is one possible demonstration of the Streamhouse architecture with Confluent Cloud products.

The home page of the application to drive the demonstration

From a business requirement point of view, the goal is to demonstrate how to synchronize a change in business state everywhere it is used.

The user story for the demonstration looks like:

as a data architect I want to deliver the business entities update to every system and person that depends on it, at the same time, so I can ensure no team operates on a stale or conflicting copy of that fact.

Streamhouse data architecture continuously captures and processes changes as they happen, governs that data, and makes the same trusted business context available to applications, agents and analytics without requiring another set of data copies and pipelines.

At the high level, Streamhouse reference architecture looks like in the figure below:

Streamhouse Capabilities

The architecture delivers a capture layer to bring data in centralized messaging platform to transport and persist records defined in structured schemas. A layer of tranformation, data enrichment and data analytics construct helps to serve golden records to downstream processing. Those golden records, representing valuable business events or data analytic products can be consumed by AI Agent to build their own, fresh, context.

When applied the architecture to Confluent technology stack, Streamhouse is supported by the following components:

Streamhouse With Confluent Cloud
  1. The capture is done by different Kafka source connectors
  2. The transport is supported by Kafka Brokers and topics, with contracts in Schema Registry
  3. Transform is done by Confluent Cloud for Flink. with stateless or stateful logic to build golden records and business events
  4. Serve is supported by Flink with snapshot queries, by Kafka Sink connectors and Tableflow to write Iceberg Tables to object storage. Real-time context engine is also a serving layer for AI Agents.
  5. Governance: is done by schema registry and other end-to-end governance capabilities.

docs.title: CDC envelop automatic processing to upsert tables
docs.text:
When created by Debezium connector the created tables have a changelog.mode set to retract if the source table in the SQL database has not primary key.

WITH (
  'changelog.mode' = 'retract',
  'kafka.cleanup-policy' = 'delete',
  'key.format' = 'avro-registry',
  'scan.startup.mode' = 'earliest-offset',
  'value.format' = 'avro-debezium-registry'
)

Still it is possible to alter the default settings so develop can work on the CDC envelop and operation. This pattern is demonstrated for the cdc.public.customers, in this SQL

 SELECT
    customer_id,
    coalesce(IF(op= 'd', before.first_name, after.first_name), 'NULL') as first_name,
    coalesce(IF(op= 'd', before.last_name, after.last_name), 'NULL') as last_name,
    coalesce(IF(op= 'd', before.email, after.email), 'NULL') as email,
    coalesce(IF(op= 'd', before.phone, after.phone), 'NULL') as phone,
    TO_TIMESTAMP_LTZ(IF(op= 'd', before.date_of_birth, after.date_of_birth), 'yyyy-MM-dd''T''HH:mm:ss.SSSSSS''Z''') as date_of_birth,
    coalesce(IF(op= 'd', before.gender, after.gender), 'NULL') as gender,
    TO_TIMESTAMP_LTZ(IF(op= 'd', before.created_at, after.created_at), 'yyyy-MM-dd''T''HH:mm:ss.SSSSSS''Z''') as registration_date,
    coalesce(IF(op= 'd', before.segment, after.segment), 'NULL')   as customer_segment,
    TO_TIMESTAMP_LTZ(IF(op= 'd', before.customer_since, after.customer_since), 'yyyy-MM-dd''T''HH:mm:ss.SSSSSS''Z''') as customer_since,
    coalesce(IF(op= 'd', before.city, after.city), 'NULL') as city,
    coalesce(IF(op= 'd', before.state, after.state), 'NULL') as state,
    coalesce(IF(op= 'd', before.postal_code, after.postal_code), 'NULL') as postal_code,
    coalesce(IF(op= 'd', before.country, after.country), 'NULL') as country,
    `$rowtime` as event_ts
    FROM {{ source('cdc', 'customers') }}

docs.title: DBT deployment, Materialized and Streaming tables
docs.text:
Confluent has developed two Python modules: dbt-confluent (adapt dbt-core to confluent cloud) and confluent-sql (Python DBAPI V2 Compatible driver to be able to run snapshot, streaming queries with different cursors).

All the flink statements presented in this repository are deployed using Confluent dbt. The project management is also complemented with other personal CLIs. See this note to review the development approach and deployment pattern using dbt

See Confluent dbt product documentation.

docs.title: Lateral snapshot join on slow moving, seeded data
docs.text:
One of common pattern within data enrichment is to join streaming record with reference data, which has lower level of change velocity. There are multiple way to support this integration, but in Confluent Cloud is it best to deploy them in Kafka topic and be able to reuse them, for any enrichment. The new lateral snapshot feature in Flink helps in join.

The seeds are defined is pipelines/seeds folder and deployed simply by doing 

dbt seed

  • seeds/country_codes.csv has 249 ISO 3166-1 countries with alpha-2, alpha-3, numeric code and name. The country_code key matches customers.country.
  • seeds/currency_codes.csv has 178 ISO 4217 currencies with code, numeric code and name. The currency_code key matches transactions.currency.
  • seeds/seeds.yml adds descriptions, plus unique and not_null tests on the two key columns

The snaphot lateral query is implemented in the transaction cdc processing

docs.title: Snapshot query
docs.text:
dbt supports running materialized table and streaming tables. The Confluent REST API exposes a run Flink statement that can also being used for snapshot query. The backend application uses the confluent sql module to demonstrate the integration inside of a human dashboard.

See this confluent client code.

docs.title: Lightning query
docs.text:
The Confluent Cloud Real-Time Context Engine (RTCE) exposes a Flink-maintained table for current-state point lookups over HTTP: a single synchronous POST returns the table's current rows in milliseconds.

The request is HTTP Basic auth with a dedicated Global resource API key (CONFLUENT_GLOBAL_KEY/SECRET, provisioned by IaC/ccloud/lightning.tf) and a body scoped by catalog_name = environment id and database_name = Kafka cluster id (IDs, not the display names the Flink SQL Statements API uses).

See Code reference

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
As a generic application behaviors:

  • Microservice applications write to database tables.
  • PostgreSQL database server
  • CDC Debezium Kafka Connector, create one topic per table, define schema in schema registry
  • A set of Flink queries prepare the data to build customer 360 analytics metrics, that are served in sink topics
  • Sink topic is processed by Tableflow to export data as Iceberg table / parquet files into object storage
  • External catalogs are in sync with Tableflow catalog
  • Web Application to support demonstrating Streamhouse capabilities

Two architectures are presented in this repository, one pure cloud, and one hybrid with local server, database, CDC to Confluent cloud Kafka cluster and Streamhouse:

Hybrid cloudCloud VPV to VPC

This is the simplest deployment to run database and code locally with Confluent Cloud for Kafka, Flink, Tableflow and Streamhouse components.

Local Database - Confluent Cloud Streamhouse

  • The postgresql server runs locally via container (on Mac - docker compose on Windows. (not yet supported)).
  • A Kakfa connector Debezium container image runs locally to CDC the 3 tables to the cdc.public.* topics
  • WebApp runs locally

The WebApp adds simple navigation, to create, update, delete customers and accounts. Transactions are creation only.

Application Customers Page

The end-to-end, more complex architecture, looks like in the following figure:

Cloud Deployment - Confluent Cloud Streamhouse

  • Application runs on EC2 host
  • PostgreSQL database server on AWS RDS
  • CDC Debezium Kafka Connector deployed as managed service
  • Kafka cluster, schema registry, real-time context engine, tableflow and Flink jobs run on Confluent Cloud

! Being more complex to deploy, this is still under construction and testing.

docs.text:
The Web App and backend to support running the demonstration has the following components:

Application High Level Component View

docs.title: Actors
docs.text:
The Streamhouse architecture offers services for three different actors:

  1. Site Reliability Engineer
  2. Data Engineer
  3. Application Developer

docs.title: SRE
docs.text:
This use case helps to demonstrate the following tasks a SRE needs to conduct to prepare the environment to support the above architecture.

There are two ways to execute those tasks, via Confluent Cloud Console or via infrastructure as Code, using Terraform. The following bullet points are generic task description that should be done using both approaches, (some are for production deployment too).

  1. Create Confluent Cloud environment, API keys and secrets, service accounts, role bindings, kakfa cluster
  2. For Production deployment create private network and network link to Confluent cloud
  3. A Schema Registry for a given environment
  4. Create Flink compute pool
  5. Create source databases, for example, a RDS service with a Postgresql instance
  6. Create Debezium CDC Source connector for DB tables using terraform
  7. Create SQL database and tables into the select database (Postgresql): accounts, customers, transactions.

This list will be updated while implementing this demonstration

docs.title: Data Engineer
docs.text:
The following steps are generic and may be supported by different tools:

  1. Create dbt project to manage Flink statements using a git repository. One of the approach is to use the star schema (see note below)
  2. Develop Flink queries using Confluent Cloud Workspace cells
  3. Save query to file in git repository, transform for dbt
  4. Deploy Flink logic using dbt cli: dbt run

This list will be updated while implementing this demonstration

We recommend organizing the Flink statements using the Star model which is a multidimensional data model to organize data in a data warehouse. It is used to denormalize business data into dimensions and facts. The fact table sits at the center of the star schema. It records the what happened, as quantitative, measurable events. The Dimension tables (The "Context") surround the fact table. They provide the "who, what, where, when, and why".

docs.title: Application Developer
docs.text:
The following steps are generic and may be supported by different tools:

  1. Define contract for data / analytics, and the methodology to engage with Data engineers as part of the microservice design
  2. Maintain schema evolution with full transitivity
  3. Integrate data in Kafka via Lightning query or snapshot queries.

This list will be updated while implementing this demonstration

  • The WebApp delivered as a MVP illustrates the integration with those new query capability to serve the data to application.

docs.title: Build Flink Processing
docs.text: This section addresses the Flink pipeline definition and management using Confluent dbt plugin.

docs.title: What is built
docs.text:
We want to implement the following pipeline to process the raw/bronze layer of records coming out of the CDC Debezium source kafka connector (cdc.*):

To a silver layer which includes clean source data, with no duplicate, reflecting a canonical model and filtered records. The golden layer includes the star schema dimensions and facts. For this demonstration the c360-profile defines analytics about a customer based on the buying transactions done so far.

The Confluent Cloud Flink statement organization reflects the medaillon and star schema structure. The Flink statements run in a compute pool, already created via the terraform deployment (or reused but referenced in FLINK_COMPUTE_POOL_ID).

  1. First, create the pipeline folder to manage the different Flink SQL statements, using the star schema pattern. This can be done manually or using a tool from flink-tools-for-agents project, which complement the dbt Confluent CLI: 

    git clone https://github.com/jbcodeforce/flink-tools-for-agents.git
cd flink-tools-for-agents
# run shift left for dbt project
uv run sl-dbt init ~/Code/streamhouse_c360_demo

    Here is the expected structure: 

    streamhouse_c360_demo
├── docs
├── IaC
├── local-tests
├── pipelines
├── sl_dbt.yaml
└── tools

  2. Add a data analytic product named c360, to keep metrics for customer 360 view. 

    uv run sl-dbt add-data-product ~/Code/streamhouse_c360_demo c360

    Here is the expected structure: 

    pipelines
    ├── dbt_project.yml
    ├── macros
    ├── models
    │   └── c360
    │       ├── dimensions
    │       ├── facts
    │       └── sources
    ├── pyproject.toml
    ├── seeds
    └── tests

  3. Add one table as output of deduplicating customers raw data, and to filter unnecessary records:

     uv run sl-dbt add-table ~/Code/streamhouse_c360_demo src_customers c360 --table-type  src

    pipelines
    ├── dbt_project.yml
    ├── macros
    ├── models
    │   └── c360
    │       ├── dimensions
    │       ├── facts
    │       ├── schema.yml
    │       └── sources
    │           ├── src_customers.sql
    │           └── src_customers.yml
    ├── pyproject.toml
    ├── seeds
    └── tests

  4. Use the Confluent Cloud Workspace to develop query by using an incremental approach: starts by selecting the different sources, to assess data quality. We will illustrate the approach for beginner.

    1. Assess the source table structure. Run the SQL: show create table cdc.public.customers

      We can observe the Debezium envelop is already transformed to the sub schema. We can verify the schema definitiom in the schema registry has a before and after envelop. Go to schema registry page and select cdc.public.customers-value. The schema has Debezium fields of before, after, op...

      The reason is the default format for the value and the key are set as: 

      value.format' = 'avro-debezium-registry'
      which means the Kafka Source connector inside Confluent Cloud Flink uses a specific deserializer that processes the envelop model.

      We can do the same for: show create table cdc.public.accounts; and show create table cdc.public.transactions;

      We can also discover that by default the changelog mode is set to retract. This is due to CDC debezium configuration that may not have defined the primary key mapping. If the Kafka topic has cleanup.policy set to compact, the changelog.mode is set to upsert instead. With retract we could not run snapshot queries but only streaming query.

    2. Look at some data and select only active customers: 

      SELECT * FROM `j9r-env`.`j9r-kafka`.`cdc.public.customers` where status = 'ACTIVE';

    3. Because the changelog mode is retract or upsert, within the topic there will be no duplicate for the current customers, accounts and transactions, the following query helps to validate that: 

       with deduped_customer as (
    SELECT 
            customer_id,
        FROM `cdc.public.customers`
    ),
    numdup as (SELECT
        customer_id,
        count(*) as num_records
    FROM deduped_customer
    group by customer_id)
    select * from numdup where num_records > 1

  5. We can continue the data analysis and finally build the following Flink SQL to do some filtering and data cleaning. See flink src processing folder.

  6. To be able to connect to Confluent Cloud, we need to set the environment variables for API keys and secrets. The following script loads those from Terraform output 

    source ./scripts/set_env_from_tf.sh

    As an alternate source the .env file under apps/backend/

  7. dbt needs models. The first layer is the references to existing CDC topics see pipelines/models/sources.yaml file.

    version: 2
sources:
- name: cdc
schema: "{{ env_var('KAFKA_CLUSTER_NAME') }}"
tables:
- name: customers
    identifier: cdc.public.customers
- name: accounts
    identifier: cdc.public.accounts
    description: accounts information for a customer    
- name: transactions
    identifier: cdc.public.transactions
    description: Topic 'cdc.public.transactions' — registered via sl-dbt get-schema-existing-topic-to-dbt.

  8. Be sure to modify your .dbt/profiles.yml with the following element. 

    cc_flink:
    outputs:
        dev:
            cloud_provider: '{{ env_var(''CC_PROVIDER'') }}'
            cloud_region: '{{ env_var('CC_REGION'') }}'
            compute_pool_id: '{{ env_var('FLINK_COMPUTE_POOL_ID'') }}'
            dbname: '{{ env_var('KAFKA_CLUSTER_NAME'') }}'
            environment_id: '{{ env_var('ENVIRONMENT_ID'') }}'
            execution_mode: streaming_query
            flink_api_key: '{{ env_var(''FLINK_API_KEY'') }}'
            flink_api_secret: '{{ env_var(''FLINK_API_SECRET'') }}'
            organization_id: '{{ env_var(''CC_ORG_ID'') }}'
            statement_label: dbt-confluent
            statement_name_prefix: dbt-
            threads: 4
            type: confluent
    target: dev

    This is a generic profile for Confluent Cloud that uses environment variables to avoid sharing secrets in yaml file.

  9. Continue to create the following flink statements to filter and transform raw CDC topics, create dimension and fact for the analytics.

The path is pipelines/models/c360

Source Table(s) Folder Name Sink Table Goal cdc.public.accounts sources src_accounts Deduplicate, flatten, filter, transform cdc.public.customers sources src_customers eduplicate, flatten, filter, transform cdc.public.transactions sources src_transactions eduplicate, flatten, filter, transform src_customers dimension dim_customers Compute customer dimension src_customers, src_account dimension dim_customers Compute transaction cross account metrics dim_customers, facts fct_c360_profiles 
├── c360
│   ├── dimensions
│   │   ├── dim_account_tx_agg.sql
│   │   ├── dim_account_tx_agg.yml
│   │   ├── dim_customers.sql
│   │   ├── dim_customers.yml
│   │   ├── dim_transactions.sql
│   │   ├── dim_transactions.yml
│   │   ├── dim_tx_x_account.sql
│   │   └── dim_tx_x_account.yml
│   ├── facts
│   │   └── fct_c360_profile.sql
│   └── sources
│       ├── src_accounts.sql
│       ├── src_accounts.yml
│       ├── src_customers.sql
│       ├── src_customers.yml
│       ├── src_transactions.sql
│       └── src_transactions.yml
├── deploy_manifest.json
└── sources.yaml

Each model needs to have the table definition to create as sink. As an example the dimension to compute account aggregations look like (file dim_account_tx_agg.sq):

models:
- name: dim_account_tx_agg
  description: "Aggregates cross account"
  config:
    contract:
      enforced: true
  columns:
  - name: account_id
    data_type: varchar(2147483647)
    constraints:
      - type: not_null
      - type: primary_key
        expression: "not enforced"
  - name: customer_id
    data_type: string
  - name: account_type
    data_type: string
  - name: account_status
    data_type: string
  - name: balance
    data_type: DECIMAL
  - name: txn_count
    data_type: DECIMAL
  - name: txn_total
    data_type: DECIMAL
  - name: last_transacted_at
    data_type: timestamp_ltz

docs.text:
dbt supports different way to manage the dependencies. We can use tag, folder, or tree.

docs.title: RDS out of storage - connection from client rejected
docs.text:
When an AWS RDS PostgreSQL instance reaches a storage-full state, AWS restricts database access and rejects standard client connections to prevent corruption.

Even without new application data being inserted, PostgreSQL can rapidly fill disk space through Write-Ahead Logging (WAL) retention, abandoned replication slots, verbose error logging, or orphaned temp files.

  • Need to scale up storage, max storage limit and current storage by +20%.

  • Connect with psql (be sure your public IP address is in the security group policy as inbound rules on port 5432) 

    export RDSHOST="c360-j9r-postgres.c......rds.amazonaws.com" 
psql "host=$RDSHOST port=5432 dbname=c360db user=dbadmin sslmode=verify-full sslrootcert=~/.ssh/global-bundle.pem"

  • Identify Why Storage Growth Occurred: Once connected via psql or your SQL client, run the following diagnostic checks:1. Check for Abandoned or Inactive Replication Slots (Most Common)If you have an inactive read replica or a disconnected CDC tool (AWS DMS, Debezium, Kafka), PostgreSQL will indefinitely hold Write-Ahead Logs (WAL) on disk waiting for the consumer to catch up. 

    SELECT slot_name, plugin, active, 
    pg_size_pretty(pg_wal_lsn_diff(pg_current_wal_lsn(), restart_lsn)) AS wal_lag
FROM pg_replication_slots;

  • If a slot has active = false and high wal_lag, drop the slot to immediately clear accumulated WAL files: 

    SELECT pg_drop_replication_slot('your_slot_name');

  • Check for long-running or stuck transactions: Uncommitted or long-running transactions prevent PostgreSQL from vacuuming dead tuples and clearing old WAL files. 

    SELECT pid, age(clock_timestamp(), query_start), usename, state, query 
FROM pg_stat_activity 
WHERE state != 'idle' 
ORDER BY query_start ASC;

  • Inspect RDS Log file accumulation: Verbose error logging (e.g., repeated connection failure loops or heavy query logging) can generate tens of gigabytes of text log files on the host. Go to RDS Console > Databases > [Your Instance] > Logs & events.

    • If log files are taking up massive space, check your DB Parameter Group and adjust rds.log_retention_period to a shorter duration (e.g., 1440 minutes / 1 day).
    • log_min_duration_statement: Increase this value (e.g., 5000 for 5 seconds) or set it to -1 to disable slow query logging entirely.
    • log_statement: Change to none or ddl (avoid all)
    • log_min_messages: Set to warning or error (avoid info or debug).
    • log_parameter_max_length: Reduce this value (e.g., 1024) to cap the size of logged query bind parameters

  • Check for file bloat: Complex queries (e.g., large sorts or joins exceeding work_mem) create temp files on disk. Aborted operations can sometimes leave orphaned temp files 

    SELECT datname, temp_files, pg_size_pretty(temp_bytes) AS temp_size 
FROM pg_stat_database;

docs.title: Demonstration Script
docs.text:
We may demonstrate the Streamhouse architecture in different ways, using one of the approaches implemented in this repository:

  1. Local database, writing directly to Kafka topics defined within Confluent Cloud Kafka Cluster
  2. Run Database on AWS, with Kafka Connector defined to get data from the database to Kafka topics. This approach has cost for the services on AWS.

For each the following activities are common:

  1. Deploy Confluent Cloud components: This step is to create Environment, Kafka cluster, schema registry, service accounts, api keys and secrets, and compute pools. We propose two approches to define the environment and components of this demonstration, one using the Confluent Console or one using Terraform:
    • using Terraform.
    • or using the Confluent cloud console
  2. Optional: Deploy Database in AWS RDS with the needed AWS components also using terraform. It includes the terraform definition to deploy Debezium CDC source connector on Confluent Cloud managed connector. This step is optional as the application can emulates CDC connector and use local database.
  3. Deploying the Flink pipeline to build the customer 360 analytics profile using Confluent dbt.
  4. See dedicated 'demo script' note to run the application with local components.

docs.title: Run with a remote database server
docs.text:
The architecture of the demonstration at the high-level looks like:

Once the Confluent Cloud and AWS resources are created by Terraform, the user starts the local web application that connect to remote database server. To do this deployment see the SRE doc

set +a

docs.title: Run with Local Database Get started locally
docs.text:
This time the database runs locally and the web app writes to kafka in parallel to write to database.

  • Be sure to have the Confluent Cloud resources created with Terraform. To do this deployment see the SRE doc

  • Start the local Postgresql server 

     ./scripts/local_start_pg.sh

    You should get some report like:

│  Local PostgreSQL connection details                    │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤

• Set where to find the specific .env file. You can use different .env file and reference it via environment variable: 

    export ENV_CONFIG_FILE=$PWD/apps/backend/.env

  • Start the local webapp

Changes written by the backend to PostgreSQL are published to the cdc.public.* topics by Debezium (see Local CDC); the backend does not produce to Kafka itself.

docs.text:
• Deploy the Flink statements using dbt

source .venv/bin/activate
# verify the version, if need to update, change in pyproject.yaml in pipelines folder
dbt version

terraform apply

Outputs:

rtce_lightning_sa_id = "sa-r2z9987"

CONFLUENT_GLOBAL_SECRET=$(terraform output -raw rtce_lightning_api_key_secret)

    or to also modify the backend .env file rerun:

docs.title: Customers Management
docs.text:
The customers page presents a list of existing customers loaded from the database:

It is possible to add a new customer, with the Add customer button, or view, update, delete an existing customer using the action icon.

For example selecting the eye icon on James Carter brings this view:

docs.title: Accounts Management
docs.text:
The accounts page presents a list of accounts per customer loaded from the database:

This view is only for demonstration purpose. It is possible to add an account, but the real use case will be to add an account from the customer view.

docs.title: Transaction Management
docs.text:
The transactions page presents a list of current transactions in the database:

Again this is for demonstration purpose.

To simulate a week of activity, click Generate 200 transactions. The backend creates 200 transactions on existing accounts, timestamped from 7 days ago in 15-minute increments, inserts them in Postgres, and Debezium publishes them to the cdc.public.transactions topic. The page then shows the newly created transactions (the list is not kept after a browser refresh).

docs.title: Data products view
docs.text:
This page demonstrates the presentation of Flink statement lineage and metrics per data analytics product.

  • First select the analytics product

  • See the pipeline graph for one of the fact table:

  • User can drill down to see real-time metrics for on of the statement, and the deployed SQL query:

    The message in and out should be greater than 0 when there is record flowing into the topics.

Recall: the architecture to support this use case is presented in the figure below:

docs.title: Analytics Dashboard
docs.text:
The Analytics page is an illustration of what can be done by directly accessing data in kafka

  1. Get the aggregation cross customers. Rather than pulling every customer row and folding it in the backend, the cross-customer aggregates are built in Flink as a CRM analytic data product — five small materialized tables (fct_crm_summary, fct_crm_by_segment, fct_crm_by_generation, fct_crm_by_gender, fct_crm_by_country) derived from fct_c360_profile. The backend reads them with five simple SELECT * snapshot queries run concurrently through the confluent-sql driver — the aggregation work stays in Flink and only the summary rows cross the wire. This is the Streamhouse pattern: build analytics products in Flink, expose them through a plain query.

    The backend also returns the elapsed time from a client point of view. A snapshot query spins up a Flink statement, so each runs in roughly 5–8s; the five run concurrently so the dashboard load is bounded by the slowest, not their sum.

  2. Use the snapshot query, which creates a Flink Statement, to get a data for a user: Same as above the query now has where condition on the customer name.

  3. We can do the same query with the new Real-time context engine, lightning query:

    We can see that it gets results in 605ms.

docs.title: Demonstrate Real-time Context Engine
docs.text:
There is a local LLM running in the background listening on http://localhost:7999/v1, so a OpenAPI compatible protocol. The backend is running an Agent with MCP tool defined in code, and the user interface support chatting with the customer 360 profile topic:

  • Examples of query to ask:
    • What is the profile of Mr Carter?
    • what about Mrs Walsh profile?
    • What is the current CRM metrics?

UNION ALL

    a.account_type, a.balance
FROM   customers c
JOIN   accounts a USING (customer_id)
LIMIT  10;

    t.merchant_category, t.channel, t.status,

docs.title: Flink Project Management
docs.text:
This section addresses the Flink pipeline definition and management using Confluent dbt plugin.

  1. To be able to connect to Confluent Cloud, we need to set the environment variables for API keys and secrets. The following script loads those from Terraform output 

    source ./scripts/set_env_from_tf.sh

    As an alternate source the .env file under apps/backend/

  2. dbt needs models. The first layer is the references to existing CDC topics see pipelines/models/sources.yaml file.

    version: 2
sources:
- name: cdc
schema: "{{ env_var('KAFKA_CLUSTER_NAME') }}"
tables:
- name: customers
    identifier: cdc.public.customers
- name: accounts
    identifier: cdc.public.accounts
    description: accounts information for a customer    
- name: transactions
    identifier: cdc.public.transactions
    description: Topic 'cdc.public.transactions' — registered via sl-dbt get-schema-existing-topic-to-dbt.

  3. Be sure to modify your .dbt/profiles.yml with the following element. 

    cc_flink:
    outputs:
        dev:
            cloud_provider: '{{ env_var(''CC_PROVIDER'') }}'
            cloud_region: '{{ env_var('CC_REGION'') }}'
            compute_pool_id: '{{ env_var('FLINK_COMPUTE_POOL_ID'') }}'
            dbname: '{{ env_var('KAFKA_CLUSTER_NAME'') }}'
            environment_id: '{{ env_var('ENVIRONMENT_ID'') }}'
            execution_mode: streaming_query
            flink_api_key: '{{ env_var(''FLINK_API_KEY'') }}'
            flink_api_secret: '{{ env_var(''FLINK_API_SECRET'') }}'
            organization_id: '{{ env_var(''CC_ORG_ID'') }}'
            statement_label: dbt-confluent
            statement_name_prefix: dbt-
            threads: 4
            type: confluent
    target: dev

    This is a generic profile for Confluent Cloud that uses environment variables to avoid sharing secrets in yaml file.

  4. Continue to create the following flink statements to filter and transform raw CDC topics, create dimension and fact for the analytics.

The path is pipelines/models/c360

Source Table(s) Folder Name Sink Table Goal cdc.public.accounts sources src_accounts Deduplicate, flatten, filter, transform cdc.public.customers sources src_customers eduplicate, flatten, filter, transform cdc.public.transactions sources src_transactions eduplicate, flatten, filter, transform src_customers dimension dim_customers Compute customer dimension src_customers, src_account dimension dim_customers Compute transaction cross account metrics dim_customers, facts fct_c360_profiles 
├── c360
│   ├── dimensions
│   │   ├── dim_account_tx_agg.sql
│   │   ├── dim_account_tx_agg.yml
│   │   ├── dim_customers.sql
│   │   ├── dim_customers.yml
│   │   ├── dim_transactions.sql
│   │   ├── dim_transactions.yml
│   │   ├── dim_tx_x_account.sql
│   │   └── dim_tx_x_account.yml
│   ├── facts
│   │   └── fct_c360_profile.sql
│   └── sources
│       ├── src_accounts.sql
│       ├── src_accounts.yml
│       ├── src_customers.sql
│       ├── src_customers.yml
│       ├── src_transactions.sql
│       └── src_transactions.yml
├── deploy_manifest.json
└── sources.yaml

Each model needs to have the table definition to create as sink. As an example the dimension to compute account aggregations look like (file dim_account_tx_agg.sq):

models:
- name: dim_account_tx_agg
  description: "Aggregates cross account"
  config:
    contract:
      enforced: true
  columns:
  - name: account_id
    data_type: varchar(2147483647)
    constraints:
      - type: not_null
      - type: primary_key
        expression: "not enforced"
  - name: customer_id
    data_type: string
  - name: account_type
    data_type: string
  - name: account_status
    data_type: string
  - name: balance
    data_type: DECIMAL
  - name: txn_count
    data_type: DECIMAL
  - name: txn_total
    data_type: DECIMAL
  - name: last_transacted_at
    data_type: timestamp_ltz

docs.title: Deploy
docs.text:
dbt supports different way to manage the dependencies. We can use tag, folder, or tree.

  • Deploy all the sources that are the first level of flink statements to deploy

dbt run --select c360.sources --full-refresh
  • Deploy the facts and its parents

docs.text:

The flink-tools-for-agents includes tools to define a manifest of metadata about existing statements and then perform deplooy, undeploy and drop tables. ```sh cd flink-tools-for-agents v # OR uv run generate-manifest --sql-dir ../streamhouse_c360_demo/pipelines/models --overwrite 
    Drop tables listed in the `drop_tables` element of the manifest
```sh
uv run flink-sql-deploy  --sql-dir ../streamhouse_c360_demo/pipelines/models drop-tables --group fraud
uv run flink-sql-deploy --sql-dir ../streamhouse_c360_demo/pipelines/models drop-tables --group crm

docs.title: Debezium CDC Setup: PostgreSQL → Confluent Cloud Kafka
docs.text: This guide configures local PostgreSQL with Change Data Capture (CDC) via Debezium, streaming database changes to Confluent Cloud Kafka.

docs.title: 1. Set Confluent Cloud Credentials
docs.text:
All the environment variables need to be defined in apps/backend/.env, which can be jumpstarted from the terraform output, via the command:

./script

docs.title: 2. Start Dev Stack with CDC
docs.text:
• Start Postgresql 
    cd IaC/local
 ./start_local_pg_server.sh

  • Configure PostgreSQL for logical replication 

    cd IaC/local
./configure_pg_cdc.sh

  • Start the Connector 

    cd IaC/local
./start_debezium.sh
# View logs
./start_debezium.sh --logs

This configuration matches the managed connector defined in IaC/connector/connector.tf.

docs.title: 3. Verify Pipeline
docs.text:
Once running, CDC captures tables in public schema. Check Confluent Cloud console for topics: - cdc.public.accounts - cdc.public.customers - cdc.public.transactions

Insert or modify data in any cdc.public.* table to see CDC events flow to Confluent Cloud within seconds (AVRO format).

docs.title: Stopping Everything
docs.text:
• Debeziun 

    # Stop Debezium
(cd IaC/local && ./start_debezium.sh --stop)

# Reset (fresh start)
(cd IaC/local && ./start_debezium.sh --reset)

  • Postgreql Server 

    # Stop PostgreSQL
(cd IaC/local && ./start_local_pg_server.sh --stop)

# Reset (fresh start)
(cd IaC/local && ./start_local_pg_server.sh --reset)

docs.title: PostgreSQL CDC Settings
docs.text:
Set in configure_pg_cdc.sh via environment or container:

  • wal_level: logical (enables CDC)
  • max_wal_senders: 4 (concurrent replication connections)
  • max_replication_slots: 4 (replication slot limit)
  • Replication slot: debezium_slot
  • Publication: debezium_pub (all tables in cdc schema)

docs.title: Debezium Connector Settings
docs.text:
Base connector config: IaC/local/debezium-postgres.conf - Matches managed connector in IaC/connector/connector.tf - Captures: cdc.public.accounts, cdc.public.customers, cdc.public.transactions - Format: AVRO (with Confluent Schema Registry) - Topic prefix: cdc

# Database connection
database.hostname=localhost
database.port=5432
database.user=dbadmin
database.password=localdevonly
database.dbname=c360db

# Replication
plugin.name=pgoutput
database.publication.name=debezium_pub
database.slot.name=debezium_slot

# Table selection
table.include.list=cdc\.\*

# Kafka output
producer.bootstrap.servers=pkc-v12gj.us-east-2.aws.confluent.cloud:9092
producer.security.protocol=SASL_SSL
producer.sasl.mechanism=PLAIN

# CDC options
snapshot.mode=initial
decimal.handling.mode=string
tombstones.on.delete=true

Runtime credentials injection: Confluent Cloud credentials are injected from environment into the runtime config:

# Required for Debezium to connect to Confluent Cloud
export CONFLUENT_CLOUD_API_KEY=<key>
export CONFLUENT_CLOUD_API_SECRET=<secret>
export CONFLUENT_CLOUD_BOOTSTRAP_SERVER=pkc-v12gj.us-east-2.aws.confluent.cloud:9092

Add these to apps/backend/.env (via ENV_CONFIG_FILE) or export in your shell before running ./scripts/run_dev.sh --cdc.

Optional PostgreSQL overrides (defaults shown):

export LOCAL_PG_USER=dbadmin
export LOCAL_PG_PASSWORD=localdevonly
export LOCAL_PG_HOST=localhost
export LOCAL_PG_PORT=5432
export LOCAL_PG_DB=c360db

docs.title: Debezium container won't start
docs.text:
Check logs:

(cd IaC/local && ./start_debezium.sh --logs)

Common issues: - PostgreSQL not running: start with ./start_local_pg_server.sh - PostgreSQL not configured for CDC: run ./configure_pg_cdc.sh - Confluent Cloud credentials missing: add to apps/backend/.env or export CONFLUENT_CLOUD_* vars - Base config file missing: ensure IaC/local/debezium-postgres.conf exists

docs.title: No messages appearing in Confluent Cloud
docs.text:
1. Verify PostgreSQL replication slot exists: 

    container exec c360-postgres psql -U dbadmin -d c360db -c "SELECT * FROM pg_replication_slots;"

  2. Verify publication captures tables in cdc schema: 

    container exec c360-postgres psql -U dbadmin -d c360db -c "SELECT * FROM pg_publication_tables WHERE pubname='debezium_pub';"

docs.title: Replication slot already exists error
docs.text:
The slot exists from a previous run. Either reset PostgreSQL or drop it manually:

container exec c360-postgres psql -U postgres -c \
  "SELECT pg_drop_replication_slot('debezium_slot');"

docs.title: AWS Resources
docs.text:
This section of the documentation is to create AWS resources for the end-to-end Streamhouse demonstration with source database, S3 buckets and Catalog.

Terraform is organized under the IaC/ directory as three independent root modules (separate local state), each file-per-concern. This split lets the core Confluent Cloud stack run locally with no AWS credentials; AWS and the managed connector are opt-in cost paths.

  • IaC/AWS/ — AWS stack: PostgreSQL RDS 17 (CDC-ready), VPC/subnet lookups, security group (allowlists Confluent egress IPs), KMS, and the Secrets Manager secret consumed by IaC/connector/. Run with scripts/tf_aws.sh as it needs AWS credentials and CONFLUENT_CLOUD_API_KEY/SECRET exported as to setup of the security group reads Confluent egress IPs dynamically.

  • IaC/connector/ — managed Debezium Postgres CDC connector on Confluent cloud: reads the core stack's outputs from ../ccloud/terraform.tfstate via terraform_remote_state, and the RDS credentials from AWS Secrets Manager. Run with scripts/tf_connector.sh (needs AWS creds). Optional — in local mode the backend app writes Debezium-shaped events directly to cdc.public.* topics instead.

Apply order: IaC/ccloud → IaC/AWS → `IaC/connector.

The resources created are illustrated in following figure:

  • RDS Postgresql instance
  • Security Group and metwork policies for the application load balancer
  • Secrets

docs.title: Pre-requisites
docs.text:
• Get Terraform cli
  • Get aws CLI

  • Get psql client to query Postgresql instance: 

    brew install libpq

  • Login to AWS console using one of your profile aved in ~/.aws/credentials 

    aws sso login --profile your-profile-name
export AWS_PROFILE="your-profile-name"

    if for any reason you do not have a profile, use: aws configure

  • Find the VPC you want to use to deploy RDS instance. For that go to the AWS Console, VPC and then select one of the VPC_id

  • Find you the public IP address of your machine: https://checkip.amazonaws.com
  • Under IaC/aws/ copy to terraform.tfvars.example to terraform.tfvars and fill in real values. 
    cp terraform.tfvars.example terraform.tfvars
    Do NOT commit terraform.tfvars to version control. IT is gitignored as of now in this repo.
  • Modify terraform environment variables terraform.tfvars for cloud region, vpc_id and my_ip_addr
  • Be sure to have CONFLUENT_CLOUD_API_KEY and CONFLUENT_CLOUD_API_SECRET exported in the Terminal session

docs.title: AWS Resources: RDS Postgresql
docs.text: The database is created in a public subnet of an existing VPC but the security group uses the user ip address to define a rule

docs.title: AWS RDS Postgresql
docs.text:
The terraform under IaC/AWS folder creates the RDS Postgresql 17 instance, with DB subnet group within an existing VPC, security group policies to restrict traffic to PostgreSQL on port 5432 within the existing VPC. The Ingress rules allow access to Postgres TCP port 5432 from VPC, client CIDRs, and Confluent Cloud egress IP addresses.

RDS storage is encrypted with KMS Customer Managed Key and DB secrets. Database credentials are securely saved in AWS Secrets Manager.

Run this stack through the scripts/tf_aws.sh wrapper rather than calling terraform directly. The wrapper handles two credential gotchas that make a bare terraform plan fail:

  • AWS: SSO profiles often store temporary (ASIA…) keys without an aws_session_token in the shared files. The AWS CLI still works from its SSO cache, but Terraform's provider rejects the incomplete set (No valid credential sources found). The wrapper refreshes the SSO token if needed and exports the full key + secret + session-token triple into the environment. It also verifies the resolved account matches the expected one (829250931565 by default; override with EXPECTED_AWS_ACCOUNT_ID) and fails fast if a similarly-named profile lands in the wrong account — e.g. 829250931565_nonprod-administrator actually resolves to 898188061957, so use AWS_PROFILE=default (or another profile in the right account).
  • Confluent: the security group ingress is built from the Confluent Cloud egress IPs, so the Confluent provider needs cloud_api_key / cloud_api_secret. Export CONFLUENT_CLOUD_API_KEY and CONFLUENT_CLOUD_API_SECRET before running the wrapper; it defensively strips any incomplete native Schema Registry / Flink env vars that would otherwise trip the provider's all-or-none validation.
# Confluent Cloud API creds must be exported (the wrapper does not read ~/.confluent/.env)
export CONFLUENT_CLOUD_API_KEY=...
export CONFLUENT_CLOUD_API_SECRET=...

# Uses the `default` AWS profile unless AWS_PROFILE is set
scripts/tf_aws.sh plan
scripts/tf_aws.sh apply
scripts/tf_aws.sh output

The output gives us the following:

db_security_group_id = "sg-...."
db_subnet_group_name = "c360-j9r-db-subnet-group"
rds_address = ".....rds.amazonaws.com"
rds_database_name = "c360db"
rds_endpoint = "....rds.amazonaws.com:5432"
rds_port = 5432
secrets_manager_secret_arn = "arn:aws:secretsmanager:....."
vpc_cidr_block = "10......"
vpc_id = "vpc-...."

Once the database is up and running, the backend creates the tables, the c360_cdc_publication, and seeds the committed CSV dataset on startup — there is no separate schema/seed script. Build DATABASE_URL from the RDS secret and run the backend bootstrap (or just start the API):

# Pull the RDS credentials emitted into Secrets Manager by Terraform
export RDSHOST="c360-....rds.amazonaws.com"
export DB_PASSWORD=$(aws secretsmanager get-secret-value \
  --secret-id arn:aws:secretsmanager:us-west-2:...:secret:c360-... \
  --query SecretString --output text | jq -r .password)

cd apps/backend
DATABASE_URL="postgresql://dbadmin:${DB_PASSWORD}@${RDSHOST}:5432/c360db?sslmode=require" \
uv run python bootstrap.py

The bootstrap is idempotent, so it is safe to re-run. The CDC publication now covers all three tables (customers, accounts, transactions).

docs.title: Use psql to verify data in RDS
docs.text:
• First get the DB password from the AWS secrets
export RDSHOST="c360-j9r-postgres.c.....rds.amazonaws.com"
DB_PASSWORD=$(aws secretsmanager get-secret-value --secret-id arn:aws:secretsmanager:us-west-2:.....:secret:c360-j9r-.... --query SecretString --output text |jq -r .password)

  • Use this to connect via psql 

    PGPASSWORD=$DB_PASSWORD psql -h $RDSHOST -d c360db -U dbadmin

  • In psql session 

    --- see all the tables in your current database
\dt
SELECT * FROM public.accounts

docs.title: Some info
docs.text:
• AWS RDS requires a DB Subnet Group. RDS manages its own Elastic Network Interfaces (ENIs). An RDS instance requires a DB Subnet Group defining a pool of subnets across at least two different Availability Zones (AZs) in that VPC (even for Single-AZ instances, so AWS can perform maintenance, failover, or migrations).
  • The aws_db_instance resource only accepts db_subnet_group_name, not individual subnet IDs

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
It is important to get the following information to be able to create the Kafka Connector for change data capture.

Resources Region us-west-2 RDS host name e.g. c360-j9r-postgres.c.....us-west-2.rds.amazonaws.com secrets_manager_secret_arn Resource ref for AWS Secrets Manager Database password Coud be created by the admin or retrieve from the secret Public certificates a .pem file to download

To retrieve password from secret, knowing the secret arn do: 

aws secretsmanager get-secret-value --secret-id arn:aws:secretsmanager:us-west-2:.....:secret:c360-j9r-rds-credentials-9x --query SecretString --output text |jq -r .password

It is possible to retrieve the secret ARN from secrets manager:

docs.title: Enhancement
docs.text: • RDS should be in private subnet with VPC private link set to Confluent Cloud

docs.title: Deploying the CDC Kafka connector
docs.text:
• Execute the following commands in sequence:
./scripts/tf_connector.sh init

./scripts/tf_connector.sh plan

./scripts/tf_connector.sh apply

  • Go to the console to verify Connector is created and running

  • And verify topics are created

docs.title: Backend does not write to Kafka

docs.title: Defining Confluent Cloud Resources with the Terraform
docs.text:
This section of the documentation is to present the exhaustive steps to deploy the Confluent Cloud components for Streamhouse using Terraform.

Terraform is organized under the IaC/ directory as four independent root modules (separate local state), each file-per-concern:

Module Purpose IaC/ccloud Core Confluent Cloud: environment, Kafka cluster, Flink compute pool, Schema Registry, service accounts + Kafka/SR/Flink API keys. IaC/AWS RDS PostgreSQL + the credentials secret (opt-in, has cost). IaC/connector Managed Debezium PostgreSQL CDC source connector (opt-in). IaC/rtce Real-Time Context Engine / Lightning Query API enablement: the Global API key + registering fct_c360_profile as an RTCE topic.

This split lets the core Confluent Cloud stack run locally with no AWS credentials. AWS and the managed connector are opt-in cost paths. The rtce module is applied last — after dbt has created the different facts tables, because it registers those existing topics with the Lightning serving layer (see Enable the Real-Time Context Engine below).

The figure below illustrates what the terraforms in IaC/ccloud/ will deploy. We start from an existing Organization, with a user with Org Admin role, and Confluent Cloud Resource API Key and Secret.

The definition helps to: * Create environment * Create Kafka cluster, Schema Registry, service account + Kafka/SR API key * Flink compute pool * Kafka topic

docs.title: Folder Structure
docs.text:
IaC/ccloud/ — core Confluent Cloud stack. Some important notes:

  • provider.tf: requires only confluent.
  • flink.tf: confluent_flink_compute_pool, no Flinks statements are those are configured via dbt.
  • outputs.tf: reports important variables to be used to set the environment variables for the application.

IaC/rtce/ — Real-Time Context Engine / Lightning Query API enablement (applied after dbt run):

  • data.tf: reads the core environment/Kafka-cluster ids from ../ccloud state via terraform_remote_state (same pattern as IaC/connector); data sources expose the cluster rbac_crn and SR resource_name for the role bindings.
  • rtce.tf: the RTCE service account, role bindings (CloudClusterAdmin on the cluster, ResourceOwner on the SR subjects), the Global API key (managed_resource kind Global), and confluent_rtce_topic.fct_c360_profile — which registers the existing topic with RTCE so the Lightning Query API serves it. Other topics are added when data engineers needs to expose new fact or dimension tables.
  • outputs.tf: rtce_lightning_api_key_id/_secret used to get CONFLUENT_GLOBAL_KEY/SECRET environment variables.

set -a
source apps/backend/.env
set. +a

The current lineage is presented by running:

dbt docs serve

The green topics are created by applications, or CDC connector.

The command below will deploy to the target environment:

dbt run --select +c360.facts.fct_c360_profile

This will create all the topics in the kafka cluster:

**Created topics by dbt"

docs.title: Enable the Real-Time Context Engine (RTCE / Lightning Query API)
docs.text:
The analytics "Customer lookup via RTCE" section queries fct_c360_profile through Confluent's Lightning Query API — a current-state point-lookup serving layer. Enabling it is a separate stack (IaC/rtce) because it must run after the table exists.

Order of operations:

  1. IaC/ccloud applied (previous sections) — environment + Kafka cluster.
  2. dbt run — creates the fct_c360_profile upsert/compacted topic.
  3. IaC/rtce applied — Global key + registers the topic with RTCE.

Prerequisites:

  • The Real-Time Context Engine / Lightning Query API Early Access feature must be enabled for your Confluent organization. Without it the Lightning API reports the org as not found (HTTP 400) regardless of this stack.
  • An OrganizationAdmin Cloud API key for the Terraform provider (creating a service account, a Global API key, and an RTCE topic are org-level operations — a resource-scoped key returns 401). This is the same CONFLUENT_CLOUD_API_KEY/SECRET exported earlier, provided it has Org Admin.
  • The fct_c360_profile topic already exists (step 2 done).

Deploy:

cd IaC/rtce
cp terraform.tfvars.example terraform.tfvars   # set prefix / cloud / region to match IaC/ccloud
terraform init
terraform apply

This creates a dedicated service account, grants it read on the cluster and Schema Registry, mints the Global API key, and registers fct_c360_profile with RTCE via confluent_rtce_topic.

Wire the key into the backend:

cd ../..                      # repo root
./scripts/set_env_from_tf.sh  # now picks up CONFLUENT_GLOBAL_KEY / _SECRET from IaC/rtce

The Lightning query is scoped by catalog_name = environment id (FLINK_ENV_ID) and database_name = Kafka cluster id (KAFKA_CLUSTER_ID) — ids, not the display names the Flink SQL Statements API uses. Restart the backend so it reloads apps/backend/.env, then the RTCE customer lookup will serve results.

docs.title: Web App and Backend Design
docs.text: This note is to explain the backend design and implementation, for code maintenance and also explaining some integration to Confluent Cloud Streamhouse capabilities

docs.title: Requirements addressed
docs.text:
• Web App to present customers page and be able to add new customer, read the detail of one customer, update one, or delete one
  • Pages for accounts CRUD operations
  • Pages for transactions CR operations
  • Local persistence with Postgresql database running in container
  • Change events published to Kafka by Debezium CDC (no backend Kafka producer)
  • TDD for backend and frontend
  • Run snapshot queries from UI to backend to Confluent cloud on top of fact tables
  • Execute lightning query from a backend and display result to Frontend
  • Chat interface to demonstrate querying business data using Real-time context engine.

docs.title: Design
docs.text:
The solution architecture looks like in the figure below:

The frontend is a classic single-page app over a REST backend.

The backend is organized in different layers to facilitate testing and adopting clear separation of concern. The structure mock a microservice implementation, which means it will be easy to separate the customer, account, transactions, analytics and chat into separate code repository and package them as 12-factors application.

docs.title: Frontend ↔ backend integration
docs.text:
The frontend (apps/frontend, React 19 + Vite + React Router) never calls fetch directly from a page. It is layered so the HTTP concern lives in one place:

  • src/config.ts — resolves the backend base URL once: VITE_API_BASE_URL ?? http://localhost:8000/api/v1.
  • src/api/client.ts — a thin request<T>() wrapper around fetch that sets JSON headers, unwraps 204 No Content, and turns non-2xx responses into a typed ApiError (reading FastAPI's { "detail": ... } body).
  • src/api/{customers,accounts,transactions,config}.ts — one module per domain, exposing typed CRUD functions (listAccounts, getAccount, createAccount, …) that map 1:1 to the REST endpoints.
  • src/types/* — TypeScript interfaces mirroring the backend Pydantic models, so the request/response contract is checked at compile time.
  • src/pages/* and src/components/* — views call only the api/ functions; they never know the base URL or status-code handling.

On the backend side, main.py mounts every domain router under /api/v1 and enables CORS for the Vite dev origin (http://localhost:5173). The browser's VITE_API_BASE_URL and the backend's CORS allow-list are the two ends of the same contract.

docs.title: Backend design pattern (models · DAO · producer · inventory)
docs.text:
Each domain — customers, accounts, transactions, analytics, chat, data lineage — is a similar vertical slice of small modules. Routing and HTTP stay thin; persistence and seeding are each isolated behind their own module:

Layer Module Responsibility API api/<domain>_resource.py FastAPI router. Validates input via the models, maps results/404/409 to HTTP. No business logic. Service <domain>/service.py Dispatch/orchestration. Delegates to the DAO. Postgres is the source of truth; Debezium publishes the changes to Kafka. Models <domain>/models.py Pydantic *Create / *Update / full models. The single schema contract shared by the API, the DAO, and (mirrored) the frontend types. DAO <domain>/db_sink.py Data-access object: the domain's PostgreSQL DDL, column list, row↔model mapping, and CRUD — built on the shared pool in db.py. Inventory <domain>/inventory.py CSV-backed seed store. Loads the committed seed CSV into typed models used to seed PostgreSQL.

Cross-cutting modules keep the slices DRY:

  • db.py — one lazily-created connection pool, a cursor() context manager (commit/rollback/return-to-pool), and reusable init_schema / seed_if_empty / CDC-publication helpers. Each db_sink supplies only its own DDL and mapping; the connection and transaction mechanics are written once here.
  • bootstrap.py — on startup (main.py lifespan), creates all tables + the c360_cdc_publication, then seeds customers → accounts → transactions in FK order, each table only if empty (idempotent).
  • config.py — environment-derived Settings (DATABASE_URL, Kafka/SR credentials, topic names).

Who owns Kafka. Debezium (local container or the managed connector on RDS) is the only producer of the cdc.public.* topics; the backend has no Kafka producer for these entities.

A new domain is added by copying the slice, registering its router in main.py, and adding its init_db + seed_from_csv to bootstrap.py.

docs.title: Database schema
docs.text:
The database has three main tables:

  • Accounts: 

        CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS accounts (
    account_id      UUID            PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
    customer_id     UUID            NOT NULL REFERENCES customers(customer_id),
    account_number  VARCHAR(20)     NOT NULL UNIQUE,

    credit_limit    NUMERIC(18, 2),            -- populated for CREDIT / LOAN accounts
    opened_date     DATE            NOT NULL DEFAULT CURRENT_DATE,
    closed_date     DATE,
    status          VARCHAR(20)     NOT NULL DEFAULT 'ACTIVE',
    created_at      TIMESTAMPTZ     NOT NULL DEFAULT NOW(),
    updated_at      TIMESTAMPTZ     NOT NULL DEFAULT NOW()
)

  • Customers 

        CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS customers (
    customer_id     UUID            PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
    first_name      VARCHAR(100)    NOT NULL,
    last_name       VARCHAR(100)    NOT NULL,
    email           VARCHAR(255)    NOT NULL UNIQUE,
    phone           VARCHAR(30),

    updated_at      TIMESTAMPTZ     NOT NULL DEFAULT NOW()
)

  • Transactions: 

        CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS transactions (
    transaction_id   UUID           PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
    account_id       UUID           NOT NULL REFERENCES accounts(account_id),
    customer_id      UUID           NOT NULL REFERENCES customers(customer_id),
    transaction_type VARCHAR(30)    NOT NULL,  -- 'DEBIT', 'CREDIT', 'TRANSFER', 'FEE', 'INTEREST'
    amount           NUMERIC(18, 2) NOT NULL,
    currency         CHAR(3)        NOT NULL DEFAULT 'USD',
    description      VARCHAR(500),
    merchant_name    VARCHAR(200),
    merchant_category VARCHAR(100),
    channel          VARCHAR(50),   -- 'ONLINE', 'ATM', 'POS', 'MOBILE', 'BRANCH'
    status           VARCHAR(20)    NOT NULL DEFAULT 'COMPLETED',
    transacted_at    TIMESTAMPTZ    NOT NULL DEFAULT NOW(),

docs.title: Query Customer Profile Facts
docs.text: To query the customer profiles directly from Kafka, there are multiple different capabilities to use. Using SQL as an interface, and Streamhouse architecture, it is possible to leverage Flink snapshot query with the Confluent Cloud REST API for flink statement, or using the new Confluent lightning query via Real-Time Contect Engine.

docs.title: Analytics Dashboard — CRM Data Products
docs.text:
The C360 analytics dashboard (KPI tiles and distribution charts) does not pull every customer row and aggregate in the backend. The aggregates are materialized in Flink as a dedicated CRM analytic data product — five small tables built from fct_c360_profile:

Table Grain Feeds in the dashboard fct_crm_summary one global row (qscope='ALL') KPI totals, averages, data-quality rollup fct_crm_by_segment per customer segment segment counts + balance-by-segment fct_crm_by_generation per generation segment generation counts fct_crm_by_gender per gender gender counts fct_crm_by_country per country country counts (top-8 + "Other")

In live mode the backend (analytics/crm_provider.py) runs five trivial SELECT * snapshot queries — one per table — concurrently through the confluent-sql DB-API driver,

and analytics/crm_aggregate.py folds the pre-aggregated rows into the dashboard payload (DataAnalytics). Only the summary rows cross the wire; the aggregation stays in Flink.

  • code involved:

  • api/analytics_resource.py

  • analytics/service.py
  • backend/analytics/providers.py
  • analytics/crm_aggregate.py to build aggregates for dashboard

Once clicking on Search the front end first goes to load customer record from the database via the customer service and resources and the get the profile by running a Flink Snapshot query to get the data out of the fact c360 profile topic/table:

This time the application logic flow leverages a client that use the REST API of lightning table:

docs.title: Real-Time Context Engine
docs.text:
This time the 'Assistant' user interface is to emulate an agent to call the Confluent real-time context engine to get real-time customer 360 profile data.

In a developer centric demonstration, we will use an harness like Claude Code, codex, pi.dev... Here we want to simulate a business user who wants to get business data directly from Kafka.

  • The frontend exposes a chat interface /pages/ChatPage.tsx with a sendChatMessage(text, history) javascript method to reach the backend via a HTTP POST to /chat

  • The backend resource api/chat_resource.py export an async function, which delegates to the service layer 

    @router.post("", response_model=ChatResponse, status_code=200)
async def post_chat(request: ChatRequest) -> ChatResponse:
  return await service.get_reply(request)

  • The service manages the support to stub mode to return canned text or live mode to run the Agno agent against the local LLM + RTCE context-engine MCP server.

  • Agno agent wires a local OpenAI-compatible LLM (an MLX server) to the Confluent Real-Time Context Engine context-engine MCP server. 
      model, server_params = _build_model_and_params()
  async with MCPTools(
      server_params=server_params,
      transport="streamable-http",
      timeout_seconds=_MCP_TIMEOUT_SECONDS,
  ) as tools:
      agent = Agent(model=model, tools=[tools], instructions=_INSTRUCTIONS, markdown=False)
      result = await agent.arun(input=prompt)
  return (result.content or "").strip()

The MCP server URL is derived from the Confluent (config.settings.rtce_mcp_url()). Auth is HTTP Basic with the org-wide GLOBAL key/secret. Agno SDK offers a set of constructs to simplify the definition of agent with prompt, tools, persistence...

It is interresting to see that a MCP ClientSession is stateful and single-session over streamable-HTTP. So the implementation uses a session, initiated from the frontend, and maintained until the user reset it. The session_id is a cache key + agno session id. Frontend generates a UUID on first submit, displays it, sends it every turn. A Reset button closes the server-side connection and starts a new UUID. Conversation continuity stays frontend-driven, the history is sent from the UI and injected into the prompt. The cache is purely connection/agent reuse for latency. Session_id also tags the agno run for visibility. The connection is lazily created on first message of a session (preserves graceful degradation), reuse until Reset. The idle-TTL is set to 30 min and a max-sessions cap evict stale ones, app shutdown closes all. Per-session lock serializes a session's turns with support to reconnect-on-failure.

Here is component view of the integration:

docs.title: Get Data Product Lineage and Metrics
docs.text:
The last part of the demonstration is to present a Flink focused lineage, with Data product view.

  • The Frontend uses a DataProductsPage and StatementGraphPage

  • The backend exposes REST resource in data_product_resource with service and provider, following previous implementation pattern.
  • As of now the list of data products come from listing json file in the descriptors folder, and each graph is a static definition from the dbt pipelines.

  • To build those json manifest there is a tool, the build_descriptors which offers a CLI to read dbt manifest.json and creates expected files for the backend: 

    cd pipelines
uv run python ../scripts/build_descriptors.py

  • To get live metrics the backend is calling the Confluent cloud REST API, and depending of the "table_type" being "streaming_table" or "materialized_table" the metrics query is not the same.

docs.title: Tests
docs.text: Both tiers are tested independently, and the test layout mirrors the module layout above — one test file per layer per domain.

docs.title: Backend (apps/backend/tests, pytest)
docs.text:
Configured in pyproject.toml (testpaths = ["tests"], pythonpath = ["."]). Fixtures live in tests/conftest.py. The suite is split so most of it runs with no infrastructure:

  • Unit / isolated — the bulk of the suite. Exercises each layer at its boundary with the dependency mocked:
  • test_*_models.py — Pydantic validation and defaults on the model contract.
  • test_*_inventory.py / test_*_seed.py — CSV load, row↔model mapping, and idempotent seeding.
  • test_*_api.py, test_cors.py — router behavior via FastAPI TestClient (status codes, 404/409 mapping, CORS headers), with the DAO stubbed.
  • Postgres integration — test_*_postgres.py. These require a live database and are auto-skipped when DATABASE_URL is unset (via the skip_without_postgres fixture / requires_postgres marker).

Seed isolation: the session-scoped isolate_seed_csvs fixture copies the committed seed CSVs to a temp dir and points *_CSV_PATH at the copies, so tests never mutate the checked-in seed files.

cd apps/backend
uv run pytest                 # unit suite (postgres tests skip without DATABASE_URL)
DATABASE_URL=postgresql://dbadmin:localdevonly@localhost:5432/c360db \
  uv run pytest               # include the postgres integration tests

docs.title: Frontend (apps/frontend/src, Vitest + Testing Library)
docs.text:
Vitest with jsdom and React Testing Library; global setup in src/test/setup.ts. Tests sit next to the code they cover (*.test.ts(x)):

  • src/api/*.test.ts — the request() wrapper and each domain client, with fetch mocked: URL/method/body construction, 204 handling, and ApiError mapping from error bodies.
  • src/pages/*.test.tsx, src/components/*.test.tsx — page and component rendering, routing, form submission, and the confirm/delete flows, with the api/ modules mocked.
cd apps/frontend
npm test            # vitest run (CI mode)
npm run test:watch  # watch mode

docs.title: Customers Frontend Implementation Plan
docs.text:
For agentic workers: REQUIRED SUB-SKILL: Use superpowers:subagent-driven-development (recommended) or superpowers:executing-plans to implement this plan task-by-task. Steps use checkbox (- [ ]) syntax for tracking.

Goal: Build a Vite + React + TypeScript frontend whose Customers page lists customers from the backend REST API with per-row view/edit/delete actions, plus separate detail and create/edit form pages.

Architecture: A React SPA under apps/frontend/. A shared AppLayout (header + left sidebar) wraps all routes via react-router. A thin typed fetch wrapper (api/client.ts) backs a api/customers.ts CRUD module consumed by the pages. The FastAPI backend gets a CORS middleware so the Vite dev server (:5173) can call it directly.

Tech Stack: Vite, React 18, TypeScript, react-router-dom, lucide-react (icons), Vitest + React Testing Library (tests), plain CSS. Backend: FastAPI + Starlette CORSMiddleware, pytest.

Spec: docs/superpowers/specs/2026-10-02-customers-frontend-design.md

docs.title: Global Constraints
docs.text:
• Frontend lives entirely under apps/frontend/ (sibling of apps/backend/).
  • Language: TypeScript. UI icons: lucide-react. No TanStack Query / axios — native fetch only. No Tailwind / component library — plain CSS.
  • API base URL resolves from import.meta.env.VITE_API_BASE_URL, defaulting to http://localhost:8000/api/v1.
  • Backend base path for customers is /api/v1/customers (do not change it).
  • Dev frontend origin is http://localhost:5173; the backend CORS allowlist must include exactly that origin.
  • Required customer fields (client validation + types): first_name, last_name, email. All other create/update fields optional.
  • Node 26 / npm 11 available. Backend managed with uv (uv run pytest).
  • Commit after each task with Conventional Commits (feat:, test:, chore:). Do NOT commit unless the executor is explicitly running under an approved execution flow; follow the repo rule "commit only when asked" — these commit steps are the intended granularity once execution is authorized.

docs.title: Review Focus
docs.text:
These are behaviors the spec implies but that no single task's happy-path test fully exercises. Each has a test pinned to the owning task below.

  • Non-2xx API response (e.g. 404 on detail, 500 on list) — the client must throw a typed ApiError carrying the status and server message, and pages must show the message, not a blank screen. (Task 3 tests the throw; Tasks 6/7 test the page display.)
  • 204 No Content on delete — client.request must not attempt response.json() on an empty 204 body or it throws a parse error. (Task 3.)
  • Create vs update dispatch — CustomerFormPage must POST when there is no :id and PUT when there is; sending the wrong verb silently corrupts data. (Task 8.)
  • Optional/empty form fields — blank optional inputs must be sent as null/omitted, not empty strings, so the backend defaults apply. (Task 8.)
  • CORS preflight/actual request from the dev origin — a request from http://localhost:5173 must come back with the right access-control-allow-origin header, or every call fails in the browser. (Task 10.)

docs.title: Task 1: Scaffold the Vite React-TS app
docs.text:
Files: - Create: apps/frontend/ (via Vite scaffolder), then prune boilerplate. - Create: apps/frontend/.gitignore (if scaffolder doesn't produce one covering node_modules, dist).

Interfaces: - Produces: a runnable Vite app with npm run dev, npm run build, npm test scripts; React + TypeScript configured.

  • Step 1: Scaffold with Vite

Run from apps/: 

cd /Users/jerome/Documents/Code/stream_house_c360_demo/apps
npm create vite@latest frontend -- --template react-ts
cd frontend
npm install

  • Step 2: Add runtime + dev dependencies
cd /Users/jerome/Documents/Code/stream_house_c360_demo/apps/frontend
npm install react-router-dom lucide-react
npm install -D vitest @testing-library/react @testing-library/jest-dom @testing-library/user-event jsdom
  • Step 3: Configure Vitest

Edit apps/frontend/vite.config.ts to add a test block and a setup file: 

/// <reference types="vitest/config" />
import { defineConfig } from 'vite'
import react from '@vitejs/plugin-react'

export default defineConfig({
  plugins: [react()],
  server: { port: 5173 },
  test: {
    globals: true,
    environment: 'jsdom',
    setupFiles: './src/test/setup.ts',

import { API_BASE_URL } from '../config'

export class ApiError extends Error {
  status: number
  constructor(status: number, message: string) {
    super(message)
    this.name = 'ApiError'
    this.status = status
  }
}

export async function request<T>(path: string, options: RequestInit = {}): Promise<T> {
  const response = await fetch(`${API_BASE_URL}${path}`, {
    ...options,
    headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json', ...(options.headers ?? {}) },
  })

  if (!response.ok) {
    let message = `Request failed with status ${response.status}`
    try {
      const body = (await response.json()) as { detail?: string }
      if (body?.detail) message = body.detail
    } catch {
      // non-JSON error body — keep default message
    }
    throw new ApiError(response.status, message)
  }

  if (response.status === 204) return undefined as T
  return (await response.json()) as T
}

import type { Customer, CustomerCreate, CustomerUpdate } from '../types/customer'
import { request } from './client'

export function listCustomers(): Promise<Customer[]> {
  return request<Customer[]>('/customers')
}

export function getCustomer(id: string): Promise<Customer> {
  return request<Customer>(`/customers/${id}`)
}

export function createCustomer(data: CustomerCreate): Promise<Customer> {
  return request<Customer>('/customers', {
    method: 'POST',
    body: JSON.stringify(data),
  })
}

export function updateCustomer(id: string, data: CustomerUpdate): Promise<Customer> {
  return request<Customer>(`/customers/${id}`, {
    method: 'PUT',
    body: JSON.stringify(data),
  })
}

export function deleteCustomer(id: string): Promise<void> {
  return request<void>(`/customers/${id}`, { method: 'DELETE' })
}

import { Eye, Pencil, Trash2 } from 'lucide-react'
import { useEffect, useState } from 'react'
import { Link, useNavigate } from 'react-router-dom'
import ConfirmDialog from '../components/ConfirmDialog'
import { ApiError } from '../api/client'
import { deleteCustomer, listCustomers } from '../api/customers'
import type { Customer } from '../types/customer'

export default function CustomersPage() {
  const navigate = useNavigate()
  const [customers, setCustomers] = useState<Customer[]>([])
  const [loading, setLoading] = useState(true)
  const [error, setError] = useState<string | null>(null)
  const [pendingDelete, setPendingDelete] = useState<Customer | null>(null)

  async function load() {
    setLoading(true)
    setError(null)
    try {
      setCustomers(await listCustomers())
    } catch (e) {
      setError(e instanceof ApiError ? e.message : 'Failed to load customers')
    } finally {
      setLoading(false)
    }
  }

  useEffect(() => {
    void load()
  }, [])

  async function confirmDelete() {
    if (!pendingDelete) return
    try {
      await deleteCustomer(pendingDelete.customer_id)
      setPendingDelete(null)
      await load()
    } catch (e) {
      setError(e instanceof ApiError ? e.message : 'Failed to delete customer')
      setPendingDelete(null)
    }
  }

  return (
    <div>
      <div className="page-header">
        <h1>Customers</h1>
        <Link to="/customers/new" className="btn">Add customer</Link>
      </div>

      {loading && <div className="status-msg">Loading…</div>}
      {error && <div className="status-msg status-msg--error">{error}</div>}

      {!loading && !error && (
        <table className="table">
          <thead>
            <tr>
              <th>Name</th><th>Email</th><th>Phone</th><th>Segment</th><th>Status</th><th>Actions</th>
            </tr>
          </thead>
          <tbody>
            {customers.map((c) => (
              <tr key={c.customer_id}>
                <td>{c.first_name} {c.last_name}</td>

import { useEffect, useState, type FormEvent } from 'react'
import { useNavigate, useParams } from 'react-router-dom'
import { ApiError } from '../api/client'
import { createCustomer, getCustomer, updateCustomer } from '../api/customers'
import type { CustomerCreate } from '../types/customer'

type FormState = Record<keyof CustomerCreate, string>

const EMPTY: FormState = {
  first_name: '', last_name: '', email: '', phone: '', date_of_birth: '', gender: '',
  address_line1: '', address_line2: '', city: '', state: '', postal_code: '',
  country: 'US', customer_since: '', segment: '', status: 'ACTIVE',
}

const TEXT_FIELDS: [keyof CustomerCreate, string, string?][] = [
  ['first_name', 'First name'],
  ['last_name', 'Last name'],
  ['email', 'Email', 'email'],
  ['phone', 'Phone'],
  ['date_of_birth', 'Date of birth', 'date'],
  ['gender', 'Gender'],
  ['address_line1', 'Address line 1'],
  ['address_line2', 'Address line 2'],
  ['city', 'City'],
  ['state', 'State'],
  ['postal_code', 'Postal code'],
  ['country', 'Country'],
  ['customer_since', 'Customer since', 'date'],
  ['segment', 'Segment'],
  ['status', 'Status'],
]

function toPayload(form: FormState): CustomerCreate {
  const out = {} as Record<string, string | null>
  for (const key of Object.keys(form) as (keyof FormState)[]) {
    const value = form[key].trim()
    out[key] = value === '' ? null : value
  }
  // Required fields are guaranteed non-null by validation before this runs.
  return out as unknown as CustomerCreate
}

export default function CustomerFormPage() {
  const { id } = useParams<{ id: string }>()
  const navigate = useNavigate()
  const isEdit = Boolean(id)

  const [form, setForm] = useState<FormState>(EMPTY)
  const [errors, setErrors] = useState<Partial<Record<keyof CustomerCreate, string>>>({})
  const [submitError, setSubmitError] = useState<string | null>(null)
  const [loading, setLoading] = useState(isEdit)

  useEffect(() => {
    if (!id) return
    getCustomer(id)
      .then((c) => {
        const next = { ...EMPTY }
        for (const key of Object.keys(EMPTY) as (keyof FormState)[]) {
          const v = c[key]
          next[key] = v == null ? '' : String(v)
        }
        setForm(next)
      })
      .catch((e) => setSubmitError(e instanceof ApiError ? e.message : 'Failed to load customer'))
      .finally(() => setLoading(false))
  }, [id])

  function validate(): boolean {
    const next: Partial<Record<keyof CustomerCreate, string>> = {}
    if (!form.first_name.trim()) next.first_name = 'First name is required'
    if (!form.last_name.trim()) next.last_name = 'Last name is required'
    if (!form.email.trim()) next.email = 'Email is required'
    setErrors(next)
    return Object.keys(next).length === 0
  }

  async function onSubmit(e: FormEvent) {
    e.preventDefault()
    setSubmitError(null)
    if (!validate()) return
    const payload = toPayload(form)
    try {
      if (isEdit && id) {
        await updateCustomer(id, payload)
      } else {
        await createCustomer(payload)
      }
      navigate('/customers')
    } catch (err) {
      setSubmitError(err instanceof ApiError ? err.message : 'Failed to save customer')
    }
  }

  if (loading) return <div className="status-msg">Loading…</div>

  return (
    <div>
      <div className="page-header">
        <h1>{isEdit ? 'Edit customer' : 'New customer'}</h1>
      </div>
      <form className="form" onSubmit={onSubmit} noValidate>
        {TEXT_FIELDS.map(([key, label, type]) => (
          <div className="form__row" key={key}>
            <label htmlFor={key}>{label}</label>
            <input
              id={key}
              type={type ?? 'text'}
              value={form[key]}
              onChange={(e) => setForm({ ...form, [key]: e.target.value })}
            />
            {errors[key] && <span className="field-error">{errors[key]}</span>}
          </div>
        ))}
        {submitError && <div className="form__error">{submitError}</div>}
        <div className="form__actions">
          <button type="submit" className="btn">Save</button>
          <button type="button" className="btn btn--secondary" onClick={() => navigate('/customers')}>Cancel</button>
        </div>
      </form>
    </div>
  )
}
